what_its_for: Colchicine is used to treat and prevent gout attacks (sudden, severe joint pain and swelling, often in the big toe). It is also used to treat a heart lining condition called pericarditis and a rare inherited condition called Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF). It works by reducing the inflammation that causes pain and swelling.
how_to_take: Take colchicine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet or capsule whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Do not crush, break, or chew the tablet. Do not take more than the amount your doctor prescribed — too much colchicine can be very harmful.
dosing: For a gout attack: The usual dose is 1.2 mg (two 0.6 mg tablets) at the first sign of a flare, followed by 0.6 mg one hour later. Do not take more than 1.8 mg over one hour during a gout attack. For preventing gout attacks: The usual dose is 0.6 mg once or twice a day. For Familial Mediterranean Fever: Your doctor will set the right dose for you, usually between 1.2 mg and 2.4 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store colchicine at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused medicine properly — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking colchicine, as it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid alcohol, as it can trigger gout attacks and increase stomach upset. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL other medicines you take — many common drugs can interact with colchicine and cause serious problems, including certain antibiotics (like clarithromycin), cholesterol medicines (like statins), antifungals, and HIV medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: muscle pain, weakness, or cramping (especially if you also feel very tired or have dark urine); numbness or tingling in your fingers or toes; pale or gray color in your lips, tongue, or palms; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of a serious allergic reaction (rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing); severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not stop; or signs of infection such as fever and chills. These may be signs of a rare but life-threatening side effect.
when_it_works: For a gout attack, colchicine works best if you take it at the very first sign of a flare — ideally within 12 to 24 hours of symptoms starting. Most people notice their pain and swelling start to improve within 12 to 24 hours of taking it. When taken daily to prevent gout attacks or treat FMF, it may take a few days to weeks to see the full benefit.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): Use with caution — older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially muscle problems. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney or liver disease: Your dose may need to be lowered or the medicine may not be recommended at all. Always tell your doctor about any kidney or liver problems. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking colchicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It may be used in certain situations under close supervision. Breastfeeding: Colchicine does pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Children: Colchicine can be used in children with Familial Mediterranean Fever. The dose will be set by the doctor based on the child's weight and age.
